chapter.title: Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal

page.h1: HTS Chapter 44: Wood and articles of wood; wood charcoal — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Tariffs on U.S. Lumber, Logs & Wood Pellets by Country (2026)
seo.shortDescription: What Canada, the UK, Mexico, China, Viet Nam, the EU and Japan charge on U.S. lumber, logs, pellets and plywood in 2026, and the approval each needs.
keywords: does canada have a tariff on us lumber

intro: What each large market charges on U.S. wood in 2026, next to what the U.S. shipped there in 2025; the EU counts as one market because its members share one tariff. For the three products that matter most, tariffs are low: logs enter every market shown free except China (10%), pellets everywhere except China and Viet Nam (3%), and lumber everywhere except Canada (25% on softwood), China (10%) and Japan (4.8% on S-P-F and pine). The costs are in panels: Canada charges 50% on U.S. plywood, and Japan 6% on plywood and OSB. For logs and lumber, the buyer’s plant-health rules usually decide more than the tariff, and for EU buyers the Deforestation Regulation from December 30, 2026.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

profile.headline: Canada buys the widest range of U.S. wood: lumber, joinery such as doors and engineered beams, logs, panels and railway ties. All of it was duty-free under CUSMA until Canada’s 2026 surtax put 25% on U.S. softwood lumber and 50% on plywood, LVL and charcoal from September 8, 2026, answering the U.S. Section 338 tariffs on Canadian wood. Hardwood lumber, logs, pellets, OSB, MDF and joinery are not on the list.
profile.mainProducts: Sawn lumber: softwood, hardwood & tropical (4407) · Builders' joinery: doors, windows, flooring, glulam (4418)
profile.tariffNow: Free (CUSMA), but 25% on softwood lumber and 50% on plywood and charcoal

regulator.name: Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA)
regulator.requirement: CFIA’s Automated Import Reference System (AIRS) gives the plant-health conditions for each U.S. wood product and state of origin. Kiln-dried lumber and panels usually move freely; logs with bark, firewood and some species from regulated U.S. areas need a phytosanitary certificate or treatment.

profile.headline: The UK is the largest market for U.S. wood pellets: fuel wood and pellets were $1.45 billion in 2025, 86% of what it buys from the U.S. in this chapter. It also buys casks and barrels ($127 million) and hardwood lumber. All three enter duty-free; for pellets, what decides sales is the UK’s biomass sustainability criteria.
profile.mainProducts: Fuel wood, wood chips, sawdust & wood pellets (4401) · Barrels, casks & staves (4416)
profile.tariffNow: Free on pellets, lumber and barrels (UK tariff)

regulator.name: Ofgem (Renewables Obligation biomass sustainability)
regulator.requirement: Power stations of 1 MW or more that burn biomass for Renewables Obligation support must meet UK land and greenhouse-gas sustainability criteria, report fuel data monthly and file an independent annual audit, so UK buyers ask U.S. pellet mills for sourcing and emissions evidence.

profile.headline: Mexico buys U.S. lumber ($398 million), mouldings, MDF, OSB, plywood and pallets, all duty-free under USMCA. Without a USMCA claim, panels, mouldings and pallets would pay 7–15%, so the certification of origin is worth getting right. Mexico has imposed no counter-tariff on U.S. goods.
profile.mainProducts: Sawn lumber: softwood, hardwood & tropical (4407) · Mouldings, flooring strips & continuously shaped wood (4409)

regulator.name: SEMARNAT / PROFEPA (forest-product import inspection)
regulator.requirement: Imported new sawn wood must meet Mexico’s phytosanitary standard NOM-016-SEMARNAT-2013, and PROFEPA inspects forest products and wood packaging at the border; logs and lumber travel with a USDA phytosanitary certificate.

profile.headline: China bought $1.62 billion of U.S. wood in 2024, mostly hardwood lumber and logs. In 2025 it added an extra tariff on all U.S. goods (125% at the April peak, 10% since May 14) and suspended U.S. log imports from March 4 to November 10, 2025. Sales halved to $806 million and part of the trade moved to Viet Nam. Lumber and logs pay 0% normally, so the 10% is the whole tariff today for buyers that use China’s exclusion process; its September 2026 Board of Trade list names U.S. hardwood lumber and logs for possible cuts.

profile.tariffNow: Normal rate (0% on logs and lumber) + 10% on all U.S. goods

regulator.requirement: Logs and lumber need a USDA phytosanitary certificate, and U.S. logs with bark must be fumigated in the U.S. (it can be recorded on the certificate); GACC re-inspects on arrival and can suspend a supplier or a whole origin after pest finds, as it did for U.S. logs in 2025.

assumptions: Rates are each market’s 2026 tariff for U.S.-origin goods: Canada’s CUSMA schedule plus its United States Surtax Order (2026), the UK Global Tariff (UK Trade Tariff, November 2026), Mexico’s USMCA schedule, China’s normal rate plus its 2025 extra 10% on U.S. goods, Viet Nam’s MFN rate, the EU Common Customs Tariff with Regulation (EU) 2026/1455, Japan’s Tariff Schedule of April 1, 2026, and the Dominican Republic’s CAFTA-DR schedule.

Each cell names the products that carry most of the trade in that heading; other lines in the same heading can pay a different rate. Where the source is WITS/TRAINS, the rate is the 2023 six-digit MFN average, and the market’s 2026 national line can differ.

Trade-agreement rates (USMCA, CAFTA-DR) apply only to goods that meet the agreement’s rules of origin and are claimed with a certification of origin; the normal rate is shown for goods that do not qualify.

Canada’s 2026 surtax applies to goods of U.S. origin under Canada’s marking rules, even when they qualify for CUSMA. China’s 2018–19 counter-tariffs answering U.S. Section 301 apply on top of the rates shown on the lines they list, unless the Chinese importer holds an exclusion; the line-by-line rates were not individually verified here.
Sanitary rules, the EU Deforestation Regulation and VAT are not tariffs and are not in the rates; the profile cards name the approval each market needs.
